title: The Things Hands Remember
subtitle: The Shore I Choose · Chapter 4 of 10
content:
There were six lanterns along the eastern footbridge, and three were broken.

Neri offered to find a carpenter. Maui offered to carry the entire bridge to a different river. I asked to see the fittings.

The first bolt came loose beneath my fingers. I took apart the little brass housing, checked the wick assembly, and sketched a safer support on the back of a flour receipt. I didn't know how I knew where the strain would travel. My hand simply drew the answer.

Maui leaned close enough to see without crowding me.

“Were you an inventor?”

“Maybe.”

“A locksmith? A shipwright? A magnificent criminal mastermind?”

“Please don't get excited about that last possibility.”

“Too late.”

It took considerably longer than my sketch suggested.

The housing was simple enough on paper: a hinge, a wick cup, a bracket, and a bolt that should have caught on the inner lip. In practice, the first lantern had been patched twice with whatever metal the village could spare. One screw had a square head; its neighbor was almost round. A thin crack ran through the support behind the glass.

Neri brought a stool and a wooden box of salvaged fittings. They knelt beside me without making the repair sound like a trial.

"We don't have much brass," they said. "The smith can make more, but not before the market delivery."

"Is this all the stock?"

"For now."

I turned a mismatched bolt in my fingers. "Then I want to test a wooden spacer instead of using two of the good ones. Only if somebody can tell me how this wood holds up in rain."

Pip, who had been carrying tools between the bakery and bridge, raised a hand.

"My granddad treats shutters with oil. I can ask what kind."

I nearly said no out of habit. It would be quicker to invent an answer than wait for one.

"Would you?" I asked.

Pip ran off, delighted to be useful.

Maui leaned over the railing. "I could fetch an entire tree."

"We need a spacer the size of my thumb."

"Very small tree."

"How about you hold the rail while I check the bracket?"

"At last. Work suited to my magnitude."

He crouched to brace the loose section. Even bent nearly double, he managed to look as though someone had invited him to a public ceremony.

The first lantern flickered when I tested it. The flame leaned toward the glass and left a trail of soot. I felt the awful urge to announce a solution anyway, because people were watching and I wanted them to stop.

"What's wrong?" Neri asked.

"Air," I said. "It doesn't have enough air coming through the lower vent. If I close the top now, it'll smoke and heat the housing."

"So the repair isn't finished."

"No."

They nodded. "Then we'll leave it unlit tonight. A warning sign is cheaper than replacing a burned bridge."

Something in me loosened. I had been expecting disappointment; what I received was a sensible answer.

Pip returned with a note from the shutter-maker and two small offcuts of treated timber. We made a spacer. I filed its edge twice and got the angle wrong once. Maui pretended not to notice until I caught him squinting at my hands.

"You may say it," I told him.

"The small tree is winning."

"Apparently."

I tried again. This time the bracket sat straight and the vent remained clear. Neri asked for a drawing of the repair so the next person wouldn't need me standing beside them. I made one, labeling every part I could name and drawing a question mark beside the fitting I couldn't.

I wanted to erase the question mark.

I left it there.

The bridge belonged to people who would cross it long after I'd gone. They deserved to know what I did not know.

By afternoon I'd repaired two lanterns and convinced Maui to stop holding pieces directly over my head. He could lift anything; that did not make him the ideal person to hold every tool.

When the third lantern lit, several neighbors clapped. I smiled, then found myself apologizing because one housing was slightly crooked.

Maui blinked.

“Why are you sorry?”

“I should have done it better.”

“It's working.”

“I know, but—”

“But what?”

I tried to answer. The remembered voice returned, without a face: If you have the ability, you have the responsibility. Don't make this about you.

My stomach tightened.

Maui's expression changed. He set down the last tool.

Neri came back with the village smith, a woman named Ressa who inspected the new fittings without praising anybody.

"The hinges are better," she said. "This one's still catching."

I felt heat climb my face. "I can redo it."

"Yes, you can. But first tell me why it catches."

She held the lantern steady while I moved the door. The brass dragged against the repaired bracket at the bottom, where I'd made the angle too narrow. I'd been so relieved that the flame was protected that I hadn't checked what happened when someone actually needed to change the wick.

Maui peered over my shoulder. "So it works, except when people use it?"

"That's an uncharitable summary."

"An accurate one," Ressa said.

I laughed despite myself. We loosened the bolt, made the adjustment, then asked a market worker to open the housing while wearing gloves. They found the catch on the first attempt and shut it again without scraping their knuckles.

"Now it works," Ressa said. She charged the council for her inspection. Neri wrote the expense down instead of turning it into a thank-you that could not buy the smith's supper.

Maui watched me sign the work sheet.

"Do your hands remember how to be pleased?" he asked.

"Apparently not."

"Could we teach them?"

"Not with a monument."

He pretended to be devastated. I looked up at the lantern we'd fixed, its new glow steadier than the old one. The work had needed another person's knowledge. It had still been my work.

"Maybe with a cup of tea," I said.

He brightened. "I can acquire tea."

"Buy it, Maui. From the person selling it."

He looked briefly offended, then grinned. We went to the stall together, and I was able to enjoy the light behind us without looking for the next mistake.

“Hey. You get to be pleased when you make something good.”

“It isn't that simple.”

“Then tell me the complicated version.”

I couldn't. Not yet.

Instead I handed him a cup of water, remembering he'd forgotten to drink while helping. He accepted it, then held it up in a mock toast.

“To the person who repaired the bridge.”

“You did the heavy lifting.”

“Yes, and I was incredible. But I'm not stealing your applause.”

That evening we crossed the bridge together. The lanterns illuminated a garden Neri had planted below. I stopped to admire a row of herbs, and Maui followed my gaze.

“You like growing things?”

“I think so.”

“Good. We'll find you a patch of ground. One you can make mistakes in without apologizing to the dirt.”

I laughed hard enough to lean against the railing.

Maui looked pleased, but a little shy when I caught him watching me. It was the first time I'd seen pride turn uncertain on his face.

“You really don't mind that I don't remember?” I asked.

“I mind that it hurts you.”

“That wasn't my question.”

“No.” He looked at the river. “I don't mind not knowing everything about you.”

“That's a first for a demigod, I imagine.”

“I contain multitudes.”

I watched the water carry the broken reflections of three new lanterns downstream.

“Thank you,” I said.

His smile softened.

“Anytime, Jasper.”

It was the first time he'd said my name without making it part of a performance. That somehow mattered more than all his grand speeches put together.
